name: Korean
intro: Learn Hangul syllable blocks and the differences among plain, aspirated and tense consonants. Final consonants and linking processes require listening; romanisation hides important contrasts. Standard South Korean usage is the main model. Professional proficiency requires sentence-ending control, honorifics and vocabulary extending well beyond introductions.

foundation.name: Korean
notes: The core inventory has 14 consonants and 10 vowels, with additional doubled consonants and combined vowels shown after them. A syllable block normally has an initial consonant and a vowel, optionally a final consonant (batchim). Initial ㅇ is silent; final ㅇ is /ŋ/.
ㄱ + ㅏ → 가 (ga); ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ → 한 (han); ㄱ + ㅡ + ㄹ → 글 (geul). Vertical vowels sit to the right of the initial consonant; horizontal vowels sit below it. A final consonant sits at the bottom.

Final consonants are restricted in sound and can link into a following vowel syllable. Nasal assimilation, tensification and aspiration alter surface pronunciation. ㄱ/ㅋ/ㄲ are distinct series; do not map them all to English k. Romanisation is a guide, not a pronunciation transcript.

Batchim letters have restricted unreleased final sounds when no following vowel links them onward. Common final categories are k, n, t, l, m, p and ng. Written final clusters include ㄳ ㄵ ㄶ ㄺ ㄻ ㄼ ㄽ ㄾ ㄿ ㅀ ㅄ. Their reading changes with the following syllable; learn a recording and a linked example instead of pronouncing both letters mechanically.
building: 한 + 글 → 한글 = Hangeul. Learn the shape of the complete syllable while recognising its letters.
먹다 → 먹어요 → 먹었어요 = eat → eat (polite) → ate (polite). Stem changes and vowel contraction depend on the verb.
책이 / 책은 versus 사과가 / 사과는. 이/가 marks a subject; 은/는 a topic or contrast. The variant depends on whether the preceding noun ends in a consonant.

sections.title: Particles and sentence organisation
sections.explanation: Korean commonly places the predicate last and omits recoverable subjects and objects. 은/는 frames a topic or contrast, 이/가 commonly marks a subject, 을/를 an object, 에 a goal/time or certain locations, and 에서 an action setting. Allomorphs depend on whether the preceding word ends in a consonant. Do not label 은/는 merely the same subject marker as 이/가.
examples: I read books in the library.
Topic, action setting and object precede the predicate.
Subject marker with a formal polite ending.
exercises: Choose 책을 or 책를.
책을. The noun ends in a consonant.
Contrast 에 and 에서 for a simple location example.
학교에 있어요 is being at school; 학교에서 공부해요 is studying at school. Other governed meanings need separate study.

sections.title: Verb forms, aspect and endings
sections.explanation: Korean predicates inflect through stems and endings. 먹다 gives 먹어요, 먹었어요 and 먹고 있어요. 아/어 selection involves vowel patterns and irregular classes. 고 있다 commonly marks ongoing action; 아/어 있다 often marks a resulting state with suitable intransitive verbs. Negative 안 and 못 distinguish ordinary negation and inability/failure in many contexts. Endings also encode speech level, connection and speaker stance.
examples: I am reading the report now.
I have not been able to check it yet.
exercises: Make a polite past form of 먹다.
먹었어요. The ending follows the stem's vowel pattern.
Why is a dictionary form not a neutral form for every conversation?
다 dictionary/plain forms and polite endings differ in function and social appropriateness.

sections.title: Noun modifiers and complex clauses
sections.explanation: Verb-based modifiers precede nouns, with forms related to time and predicate type: 읽는 책, 읽은 책, 읽을 책. Descriptive predicates have their own modifier patterns. Nominalisation with 기 or 것 permits propositions to occupy noun-like roles. Connectors such as 지만, 때문에 and 으면 relate contrast, reason and condition; learn their restrictions and register.
examples: If the conditions change, the result changes too.
exercises: What is the head of 어제 읽은 논문?
논문. The preceding phrase specifies it.
Build a contrast with 지만.
결과는 흥미롭지만 추가 확인이 필요합니다. The results are interesting, but further checking is needed.

sections.title: Honorifics and professional interaction
sections.explanation: Subject honorific 시, honorific vocabulary and speech levels are separate dimensions. A formal polite ending alone does not establish correct treatment of every participant. 드리다 and 주다 differ in the relation of giving; 말씀 can replace 말 in respectful contexts. Identify the agent and recipient before choosing an honorific form. Workplace norms vary by organisation and relationship.
examples: Formal courteous request with subject honorific.
I will send you the materials.
드리다 frames an action directed respectfully to the recipient.
exercises: What should a professional phrase note record?
Who says it to whom, the action agent, speech level and a complete example.
Write a clarification request.
이 표현의 의미를 조금 더 자세히 설명해 주시겠습니까? Request detail while maintaining an appropriate relationship.

sections.title: Academic reading and careful claims
sections.explanation:
Research vocabulary includes 연구 study, 방법 method, 결과 result, 근거 grounds/evidence and 한계 limitation. Formal written sentences often compress information into noun phrases.
Teaching passage: 이 결과는 두 요인 사이의 관련성을 보여 준다. 그러나 한 요인이 다른 요인의 원인임을 증명하는 것은 아니다. 결론을 평가하려면 연구 조건을 확인해야 한다.
Translation: This result shows an association between two factors. However, it does not prove that one is the cause of the other. Evaluating the conclusion requires checking the study conditions.
examples: does not prove that it is the cause
Nominalised proposition and a carefully scoped negative.
in order to evaluate / if one intends to evaluate
exercises: Distinguish 보여 주다 from 증명하다 in the passage.
The former indicates/shows a relation; the latter claims proof. The passage denies proof of causation.
Produce a 100-word professional summary.
Check noun modifiers, referents, formal consistency and the strength of the causal claim.

rules.title: Topic 은 and 는
rules.explanation: 은/는 marks topic or contrast. 은 follows a consonant-final noun; 는 follows a vowel-final one. The grammatical subject can be marked separately within a topic-comment structure.

examples.translation: I'm going to go.

examples.native: 톰은 벽장에서 헌 구두상자를 꺼내 열었다.
examples.translation: Tom pulled out an old shoebox from his closet and opened it.

examples.native: 너는 분명히 재능이 있는데 더 많이 못 배워서 아쉽구나.
examples.translation: You have talent, no doubt; it's just a pity that you haven't learned more.

rules.title: Subject 이 and 가
rules.explanation: 이/가 commonly marks a subject or focused identification. The variant follows the preceding noun’s final sound. These syllables can also appear inside lexical forms, so check the phrase boundary.

examples.translation: I feel guilty.
British films are better than American films.
It's out of the question.

rules.title: Object 을 and 를
rules.explanation: 을/를 marks many direct objects. 을 follows a consonant, 를 a vowel. It is often dropped in casual speech when the relationship remains clear.

examples.native: 연필을 입에 넣지 마세요, 실수로 입천장을 찌를 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: Don’t put a pencil in your mouth. You might accidentally stab your palate.
How many times do I need to repeat it?
He kept me waiting.

rules.title: Destination and location 에
rules.explanation: 에 marks many destinations, times and locations with existence predicates. Event location often uses 에서 instead. The predicate determines the appropriate relation.

examples.native: 나 오늘밤 너의 파티에 가도 돼?
examples.translation: Can I come to your party tonight?
Tom was sitting in the garden.
For the first time in ages, I slept late.

rules.title: Event location and source 에서
rules.explanation: 에서 often marks where an action happens or where movement originates. It contrasts with location 에 for many state/existence predicates.

examples.native: 외국에서 살면서 좀 불편한 건 없었어?
examples.translation: Don't you feel any inconvenience living abroad?

examples.native: 톰과 메리는 스마트 홈에서 거주하고 있어요.
examples.translation: Tom and Mary live in a smart home.
I don't know where this came from.

rules.title: Recipient markers
rules.explanation: 에게/한테 mark many animate recipients; 께 is honorific. Register and the person’s status influence the choice. Inanimate destinations often take another marker.

examples.native: 그녀는 고급 진과 토닉 한 잔은 여름과도 같다고 했다, 그리고 그것은 나에게 진실함을 느끼게 해주었다.
examples.translation: She said that a good gin and tonic is like summertime in a glass, and it struck me as being too true.
I texted Tom back.
I'll give this to Tom.

rules.title: Possession 의
rules.explanation: 의 links a possessor or modifier to a following noun. It is often reduced or omitted in familiar phrases. Pronunciation can differ from the spelling in possessive use.

examples.translation: Tom is a pioneer in this field.

examples.native: 독서는 더 이상 소수의 전유물이 아니게 되었다.
examples.translation: Reading books ceased to be a privilege of a minority.
What kind of work do you do?

rules.title: Inclusion 도
rules.explanation: 도 commonly means also/even. Its scope is the expression it follows, and it often replaces an ordinary subject/object marker.

examples.translation: The gift was still wrapped.
She is more beautiful than any other girl.

examples.native: 여기는 이주 전부터 비가 하나도 오지 않았다.
examples.translation: There has been no rain here for the past two weeks.

rules.title: Restriction 만
rules.explanation: 만 restricts a phrase to only. It can combine with case particles. Restriction and inclusion change the statement’s meaning even when both alternatives are grammatical.

examples.native: 해결책을 찾았지만 너무 빨리 찾아서 맞는 답이 아닌거 같습니다.
examples.translation: I found a solution, but I found it so fast that it can't be the right solution.

examples.native: 그녀가 미소지을 땐, 녹아내릴 것만 같아.
examples.translation: When she smiles, I feel like melting.

examples.native: 톰은 획기적이지는 않지만 좋은 영화는 잘 만든다.
examples.translation: Tom doesn't innovate, but he does make good movies.

rules.title: Formal polite endings
rules.explanation: Formal polite endings serve statements and questions with related forms. The stem’s shape and predicate type determine the ending. Formal style is not the only polite style.

examples.translation: Today is June 18th and it is Muiriel's birthday!
Muiriel is 20 now.
Children are not allowed in.

rules.title: Conversational polite endings
rules.explanation: The 해요 style is polite and common in everyday conversation. Stem vowels and contractions affect -아요/-어요 selection. Copulas have their own 이에요/예요 forms.

examples.native: 벌써 우리가 만난 지 4년 이에요. 시간이 참 빠른 것 같아요.
examples.translation: It's already been 4 years since we met. How time flies.
I want to learn Korean.
Does John want to see a Korean movie?

rules.title: Past forms
rules.explanation: Past -았/었- combines with a stem and a speech-level ending. Contractions are frequent, including 하다→했-. Retain the intended level of politeness when changing tense.

examples.translation: Tom hasn't decided yet.
Yuriko Himekusa committed suicide.
I really wanted to help.

rules.title: Negation
rules.explanation: 안 commonly negates; 못 commonly expresses inability or failure to perform. Their placement and long-form alternatives depend on the predicate and register.

examples.translation: One must not abuse animals.

examples.native: 저 두 명은 사이가 안 좋다.
examples.translation: Those two don't get along.
I don't drink that without sugar.

rules.title: Existence and absence
rules.explanation: 있다 and 없다 express existence/absence and some possession. Their complements do not behave exactly like English have objects. Location and subject marking remain important.

examples.translation: Not wanting is the same as having.

examples.native: 다른 사람을 귀찮게 할 수 있다.
examples.translation: The others can't be bothered.

examples.native: 새로운 친구를 만드는 건 어려울 수 있다.
examples.translation: It can be hard to make new friends.

rules.title: Progressive forms
rules.explanation: A verb stem plus -고 있다 often marks ongoing activity. Some result-state readings require another pattern. The lexical verb and context determine aspect.

examples.native: 톰은 수년 간 우울증과 싸우고 있어.
examples.translation: Tom has been battling depression for many years.
Tom and I are house hunting.
I look forward to it.

rules.title: Conditional linking
rules.explanation: -(으)면 builds a conditional relation. The stem’s final consonant determines the linking form. It can express a real or hypothetical situation according to context.

examples.translation: Too many cooks spoil the broth.

examples.native: 톰이 네가 이걸 하는 걸 본다면 울게 될 걸.
examples.translation: If Tom saw you doing that, he'd cry.

examples.native: 너 그 사람을 오빠-동생으로 생각하니? 아니면 애인으로 사랑하니?
examples.translation: Do you love him like a brother or do you love-love him?

rules.title: Cause and sequence
rules.explanation: These connective endings express reason, sequence or another relation depending on context. They have restrictions on following commands and proposals; learn the whole construction.

examples.native: 어제 너무 많이 먹어서 이제 난 병이 나요.
examples.translation: Yesterday I ate too much and now I feel sick.

examples.native: 니가 좀 외로울 것 같아서 내가 와인 한 병을 들고 왔지.
examples.translation: I thought you might be lonely, so I came over with a bottle of wine.
It's cold today, so wear thick clothes.

rules.title: Contrast and coordination
rules.explanation: -지만 marks contrast/concession; -고 often links predicates. Tense and subject interpretation can depend on the linked clauses rather than an English word-for-word connector.

examples.translation: Where do you want to go?

examples.native: 개는 잘 짖는 다고 좋은 개가 아니다.
examples.translation: A dog who is a good barker is not a good dog.
That's all I'm doing.

rules.title: Requests and honorific endings
rules.explanation: -(으)세요 commonly forms polite requests and also contains honorific subject marking in other uses. -(으)십시오 is more formal. Respectful reference and polite address are related but separate choices.

examples.translation: Don't you lie!
One more bottle of wine, please.

examples.native: 혹시 불분명한 점이 있을 경우 연락 주십시오.
examples.translation: In case something is not clear, please contact us.

rules.title: Questions and stance
rules.explanation: Question words ask for specific information. 아마 marks a probability/guess rather than a question. Sentence endings communicate stance and relationship; do not translate only the lexical words.

examples.translation: What are you doing right now?
Where can I make a phone call?
Where is the bank?

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
